title: NCAR's DICast wind forecasts cut Xcel Energy's forecast error to 10.8%; Xcel estimates US$49 million saved
summary: NCAR's adaptive forecast-blending system (DICast), used by Xcel Energy since 2009, cut mean wind forecast error from about 18% to 10.8% by 2014; Xcel estimated US$49m saved (IEEE Spectrum 2015).
account: NCAR's wind power forecasting system for Xcel Energy blends numerical weather models with the Dynamic Integrated foreCast (DICast) system. DICast constantly checks its predictions against outcomes and adjusts its bias corrections and weightings. The Xcel, NREL and UCAR authors of a 2011 NREL report state that the NCAR system entered Xcel's operations between November 2009 and April 2010. They found that day-ahead error at Public Service Company of Colorado fell from 18% in 2009 to 14.3% in 2010. A UCAR news item (7 February 2012) said that the system saved ratepayers $6 million in 2010 alone. It described the work as building on NCAR research ranging from statistics to artificial intelligence. MIT Technology Review (23 April 2014) described the software as artificial-intelligence-based and reported that the forecasts saved Xcel nearly as much money in 2013 as in the three previous years combined. Sue Ellen Haupt and William Mahoney of the National Center for Atmospheric Research wrote in IEEE Spectrum (22 October 2015) that DICast had been used for wind prediction since 2009. The mean forecast error at a typical wind farm fell from about 18 percent in 2008 to 10.8 percent by 2014. Xcel estimated that the improvements had saved customers US$49 million so far. E&E News (4 December 2017) quoted Haupt as saying that the forecasts could save $10 million a year. It reported that Xcel operators decommit large coal units when sustained wind is predicted. None of the sources describes the system as machine learning in so many words. The savings are Xcel's estimates, reported through NCAR and the press, and no regulator has audited them.
purpose: The National Center for Atmospheric Research built the system to forecast wind generation, so that Xcel could decide which generating units to commit and what electricity to trade. Cost savings were the intended result.
system: NCAR wind power forecasting system with the DICast adaptive forecast blending engine
developer: National Center for Atmospheric Research (Research Applications Laboratory)

ratings.reason: The NCAR authors report that forecast error at a typical wind farm fell from about 18% of capacity in 2008 to 10.8% in 2014, a measured gain in accuracy. The savings figures are Xcel's estimates.

data.answer:
NCAR's adaptive forecast-blending system (DICast), used by Xcel Energy since 2009, cut mean wind forecast error from about 18% to 10.8% by 2014; Xcel estimated US$49m saved (IEEE Spectrum 2015).

Forecast error improved, while Xcel's cumulative US$49 million saving remains an attributed estimate. The adaptive weighting description does not establish exactly which learned technique generated the gain. The later US$10 million annual estimate is not an independent verification of the cumulative total.

The forecasting system's contribution to savings is Xcel's own estimate relayed by NCAR authors and reporters. The AI character of the system rests on UCAR's reference to artificial-intelligence research and DICast's adaptive bias correction, not on an explicit machine-learning description. So both the AI status and the causal share are unverified.

The 2011 NREL report has authors from Xcel, NREL and UCAR. E&E News quotes Haupt, and MIT Technology Review quotes Xcel dispatchers and managers. The savings figures are Xcel's estimates, reported through NCAR and the press.

fields.summary: NCAR's adaptive forecast-blending system (DICast), used by Xcel Energy since 2009, cut mean wind forecast error from about 18% to 10.8% by 2014; Xcel estimated US$49m saved (IEEE Spectrum 2015).
fields.account: NCAR's wind power forecasting system for Xcel Energy blends numerical weather models with the Dynamic Integrated foreCast (DICast) system. DICast constantly checks its predictions against outcomes and adjusts its bias corrections and weightings. The Xcel, NREL and UCAR authors of a 2011 NREL report state that the NCAR system entered Xcel's operations between November 2009 and April 2010. They found that day-ahead error at Public Service Company of Colorado fell from 18% in 2009 to 14.3% in 2010. A UCAR news item (7 February 2012) said that the system saved ratepayers $6 million in 2010 alone. It described the work as building on NCAR research ranging from statistics to artificial intelligence. MIT Technology Review (23 April 2014) described the software as artificial-intelligence-based and reported that the forecasts saved Xcel nearly as much money in 2013 as in the three previous years combined. Sue Ellen Haupt and William Mahoney of the National Center for Atmospheric Research wrote in IEEE Spectrum (22 October 2015) that DICast had been used for wind prediction since 2009. The mean forecast error at a typical wind farm fell from about 18 percent in 2008 to 10.8 percent by 2014. Xcel estimated that the improvements had saved customers US$49 million so far. E&E News (4 December 2017) quoted Haupt as saying that the forecasts could save $10 million a year. It reported that Xcel operators decommit large coal units when sustained wind is predicted. None of the sources describes the system as machine learning in so many words. The savings are Xcel's estimates, reported through NCAR and the press, and no regulator has audited them.
